checkpoints: Chat app → Firestore Native for realtime message push: Firestore's realtime listeners deliver instant updates without polling; Bigtable has no push/listener mechanism at all, so swapping it in would need an extra pipeline (Pub/Sub or polling) just to fake realtime.
Firestore also ships an offline-first SDK for mobile/web that auto re-syncs once a device reconnects — a further reason it fits the chat app.

Throughput range: Firestore's effective serving range comfortably covers 500 QPS but isn't built to sustain tens of thousands of writes/sec continuously; Bigtable is purpose-built for exactly that (>10k writes/sec sustained), which is why it — not Firestore — must handle the IoT system's 20k+ writes/sec.
IoT access pattern → Bigtable: the workload only needs row-key range scans (row key designed from device ID + timestamp), not realtime listeners or complex multi-field queries.

Cannot swap — Firestore's cost model: per-operation billing suits moderate, uneven traffic; running 20,000 writes/sec continuously would send the bill through the roof with no bulk-discount mechanism.
Cannot swap — Bigtable's cost model: fixed per-node-hour pricing regardless of QPS is only cost-effective at high utilization, so a 500 QPS chat app would waste most of a node's capacity.
Overall principle: the choice is driven by access pattern (need for push/instant updates, throughput level) matched to the corresponding pricing model, not by which service sounds more powerful.
Disagree with the architect's claim — a Cloud SQL read replica is not a valid DR mechanism because it relies on async replication, which gives no RPO=0 guarantee.
Mechanism of async replication: the primary commits a write first and only afterward sends the change to the replica; lag is typically under 100ms but can spike to several seconds under load.

If the primary dies suddenly (a hard crash or VM loss, not a graceful shutdown), the replica can be missing the last unreplicated writes, so promoting it means accepting real data loss rather than a seamless handover.
The correct DR mechanism is HA mode (`availability_type = "REGIONAL"`), not the read replica.

HA mode works via a regional persistent disk replicated synchronously at the storage layer across two zones in the same region — fundamentally different from database-level streaming replication between separate instances.
Because replication is synchronous at the storage layer, RPO is genuinely zero — every committed write exists in both zones before the response returns to the client.
On primary failure, Google attaches the disk image to the standby VM and restarts the database, giving an RTO of roughly 30–60 seconds.

Redesign: keep the read replica doing its real job of scaling reads (e.g., routing 80% of read traffic to it) while relying on HA mode for actual DR — the two mechanisms solve different problems and cannot substitute for one another without accepting data-loss risk.
Instance never died — `READY` status and correct provisioned RAM prove the instance is still alive, not crashed.
`OOM command not allowed` is Redis's own write-refusal error (Redis choosing to reject the write), not the Linux OOM-killer — so the app's "Redis is dead" diagnosis is wrong.

Root cause: `redis_configs` is not declared in the Terraform config, so Memorystore falls back to Redis's default `maxmemory-policy = noeviction`, which refuses new writes once RAM hits the `maxmemory` limit instead of evicting keys.

`noeviction` is correct when Redis is a store with its own source of truth (durable queue, counter), but wrong for a cache-aside layer, which must always accept new writes and evict old keys to make room.

This explains the "weeks of running fine" timing: the cache gradually filled toward the 5GB limit as each expensive query added an entry and nothing ever evicted, until it hit the limit and every new `SET` started being refused.
Fix: add `redis_configs = { "maxmemory-policy" = "allkeys-lru" }` (or `allkeys-lfu` for frequency-based eviction) to the resource so Redis evicts the least-used key when RAM is full.
Verify the config took effect with `redis-cli config get maxmemory-policy` returning the new value.
Verify the fix actually works by loading more keys past 5GB and confirming `INFO stats` shows `evicted_keys` climbing instead of `OOM command not allowed` reappearing.

Verdict: KHÔNG approve merge ở trạng thái hiện tại — "already partitioned by day" chỉ là điều kiện CẦN, không phải ĐỦ cho việc tối ưu chi phí; review comment phải nêu rõ cả hai bug, không dừng lại ở "đã partition, ổn rồi".
Bug 1 (schema): `time_partitioning` không set `require_partition_filter = true` (mặc định là `false`), nghĩa là BigQuery vẫn CHO PHÉP một query không có bất kỳ filter nào trên `event_date` chạy được.

Bug 2 (sample query): query mẫu của team filter theo `user_id` và sort theo `event_date` nhưng KHÔNG có `WHERE event_date = ...` hay bất kỳ điều kiện nào trên cột partition — với bảng 100 TB, thiếu điều kiện này nghĩa là quét toàn bộ mọi partition.

Vấn đề `SELECT *`: vì BigQuery storage là columnar, `SELECT *` quét TOÀN BỘ các cột được lưu trữ, trong khi dashboard chỉ thực sự cần một vài field hiển thị — nếu bảng có hàng chục cột, việc này khiến lượng quét lớn hơn nhiều lần so với liệt kê đúng các cột cần.

Tác động chi phí kết hợp: mỗi lần chạy query mẫu này quét gần như toàn bộ 100 TB × mọi cột — tốn vài trăm USD, lặp lại MỖI SÁNG, mà không ai nhận ra vì query vẫn trả về kết quả đúng, chỉ là tốn kém một cách vô hình.

Fix 1: thêm `require_partition_filter = true` vào schema — bất kỳ query nào thiếu filter trên `event_date` sẽ bị BigQuery TỪ CHỐI ngay lập tức thay vì âm thầm bị tính phí, buộc team viết query đúng ngay từ đầu.
Fix 2a (khớp Bug 2): sửa lại query mẫu, thêm điều kiện `WHERE event_date >= ...` khớp đúng khoảng thời gian dashboard cần, thay vì để query quét mọi partition.

Fix 2b (khớp lỗi `SELECT *`): liệt kê đúng các cột dashboard thực sự cần thay vì `SELECT *`; cân nhắc thêm `cluster_by` trên `user_id` nếu filter theo user là pattern phổ biến, giúp BigQuery thu hẹp phạm vi quét hơn nữa trong mỗi partition.

Identifies flaw 1 — routing every object straight to Archive on upload ignores GCS's per-class minimum storage duration (Nearline 30 days, Coldline 90 days, Archive 365 days); deleting or switching class before that threshold triggers the early-delete penalty, where GCS still charges for the remaining minimum-duration time even though the object is gone.

Explains the practical consequence for invoices: real invoices often need correcting or voiding within the first few months (before the dispute window closes), so if objects jump straight into Archive on upload, every edit/delete within the first 365 days gets hit with the early-delete penalty — turning the intended storage savings into extra penalty fees during exactly the phase that needs the most editing.

Identifies flaw 2 (the more serious one) — enabling `lock_retention = true` immediately is an irreversible action: once locked, the retention policy can never be shortened or removed by any means, not even by the project owner.

Explains the risk of locking on day one: if the retention duration was entered wrong (misunderstood legal requirement, or the final compliance requirement wasn't yet settled), the team is stuck with that wrong config for the full 10 years with no way back.

Redesigns the lifecycle to match the invoice's real phases: keep Standard/Nearline for the first 90–180 days (matching the business dispute/correction window), then cascade to Coldline, and only move to Archive once the invoice is guaranteed fully "frozen" (usually after 1 year) — avoiding the early-delete penalty during the still-volatile phase.

Redesigns the retention approach: set `retention_policy` with the required day count but do NOT lock it initially — let it run, review the day count and behavior with legal/finance, and only enable `lock_retention = true` once absolutely certain, since locking on the very first apply has no undo.
Add date partitioning on `event_date` (`time_partitioning`, DAY granularity) so that queries filtering by the last 1–7 days scan only the relevant partitions instead of the full 50 TB history.
Add clustering on `customer_id` so that within each day's partition, BigQuery further narrows the scan to the specific customer instead of reading every customer's data for that day.

Set `require_partition_filter = true` as a mandatory guardrail — without it, a single query that omits the date filter still runs and silently rescans the entire 50 TB, undoing the partitioning/clustering benefit.

Recognize that the workload's steady, predictable, continuous pattern (~10 TB/month ingested, business-hours usage) is the correct signal to consider switching from on-demand pricing to a slot reservation (flat-rate) model — flat-rate pays off under high steady utilization but is a poor fit for spiky/erratic workloads.

Sequence the changes correctly: apply partitioning/clustering first and re-measure actual bytes-scanned/cost on the new baseline before sizing or committing to a slot reservation, since committing off the old unoptimized baseline would lock in a fixed price sized for artificially inflated demand caused by unnecessary full scans.

Validate the optimization's effect directly — run `bq query --dry_run` (or query `INFORMATION_SCHEMA.JOBS`) on representative queries and compare `totalBytesProcessed` before vs. after — rather than waiting until the end of the month to check the bill.
All three lifecycle_rule blocks use action.type = "SetStorageClass" (not "Delete"), so the object stays alive and only its storage class changes throughout the cascade.
The three rules set storage_class to NEARLINE, COLDLINE, and ARCHIVE respectively, paired with condition.age of 30, 90, and 365.

condition.age is always the number of days since the object's creation time, never since the previous storage-class switch — so the thresholds 30/90/365 share the same origin, and treating them as sequential offsets (30, then 120, then 485) is the common miscalculation, since that would contradict "Coldline after 90 days since creation."
Each rule is evaluated independently every day, checking the object's current age against its own condition to decide whether to apply its action.
States the resulting cascade timeline: Standard for days 0-29, Nearline for days 30-89, Coldline for days 90-364, Archive from day 365 onward.
The object always ends up in the latest/highest class whose rule matches, because storage class can only advance forward via the next matching rule, never jump backward.

Nêu được vì sao không có "nơi gắn policy" trên GCP: mô hình cấp quyền của GCP khác hoàn toàn AWS — AWS coi policy là một JSON document độc lập rồi "attach" vào user/role, còn GCP không có khái niệm document độc lập kiểu đó.

Giải thích đơn vị cấp quyền trên GCP là "binding": gắn một role (tập hợp permission, ví dụ roles/compute.instanceAdmin.v1) cho một member (user/group/service account) tại một cấp cụ thể trong resource hierarchy (resource → project → folder → organization).

Nêu được cách tìm đúng theo tư duy GCP: thay vì tìm chỗ "attach cho SA", phải mở trang IAM của resource/project và xem danh sách "ai có role gì ở đây", SA chỉ là một member row trong danh sách binding đó.
Giải thích effective policy trên một resource là tổng cộng dồn (additive) của mọi binding trực tiếp trên resource đó cộng với mọi binding kế thừa từ folder/project/organization phía trên.
Nêu được binding thông thường không có "deny", chỉ có allow cộng dồn — khác với AWS nơi một Deny tường minh có thể override Allow trong cùng policy document.

Giải thích ba resource Terraform (google_project_iam_member, google_project_iam_binding, google_project_iam_policy) đều thao tác trên cùng khái niệm binding chứ không phải ba API "policy" riêng biệt như tư duy AWS mong đợi, và nêu được mức độ rủi ro tăng dần theo phạm vi ghi đè: _member chỉ thêm một binding (an toàn khi nhiều team cùng quản lý một project), _binding ghi đè toàn bộ member của một role (dễ vô tình xoá quyền team khác đã gán), _policy ghi đè toàn bộ policy của resource (rủi ro nhất).

A JSON key is a long-lived credential that never expires on its own — once downloaded to a personal machine it exists indefinitely until someone actively revokes it; if it leaks (accidentally committed to a git repo even if private, copied off a lost/compromised personal machine, or accidentally logged), an attacker gets that SA's permissions indefinitely, unlike a temporary token that self-invalidates after a short time.
Granting roles/owner — the highest permission on the project — for a task that's just deploy is a serious least-privilege violation (overly broad scope for what's needed).
If the leaked key carries owner role, the blast radius is the entire project (deleting resources, changing IAM, accessing all data), not limited to the deploy scope.
Proposed replacement: service account impersonation, where the dev signs in with their own personal identity (gcloud auth login) rather than using a downloaded key file.
The dev is granted exactly one permission on the target SA — roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator — not the SA's business permission directly.
The SA itself still holds the business permission needed for the deploy, ideally scoped narrower than owner rather than granted straight to the dev.

When the script needs to run, the dev calls the generateAccessToken API to mint a short-lived access token (at most 3600 seconds) representing that SA, used once and then gone, so no credential file sits around long enough to leak.

This separates identity from permission: business permission stays centralized and auditable on the SA, while the dev's personal identity only holds the ability to impersonate — revoking access is just removing the Token Creator binding, with no key rotation/revocation dance needed.
This is NOT an IAM misconfiguration — the developer's `roles/owner` is fully intact and already grants sufficient permission to call the API for creating the GCE instance.

GCP enforces two separate, perpendicular guardrail layers — IAM and Org Policy — each answering a different question: IAM governs "WHO is allowed to CALL which API" (identity/action), while Org Policy governs "what SHAPE a resource is allowed to have."

A concrete Org Policy constraint like `compute.vmExternalIpAccess` can forbid every VM in a project/folder/org from getting an external IP, regardless of who creates it — this is the layer that's actually blocking the request here.
A request only succeeds if it passes BOTH layers: IAM must allow the call, AND the resource's shape must comply with Org Policy.

No matter how powerful `roles/owner` is, it cannot override or bypass Org Policy, because the two mechanisms are deliberately designed to be independent — this prevents one overly powerful permission from silently breaking an org-wide security/compliance guardrail.
Conclusion: the block is the guardrail working exactly as designed, not a bug that should be "fixed" by adjusting the developer's IAM permissions.
The correct fix is changing the Org Policy itself — not the developer's IAM — at the appropriate level (project/folder/org).

That change typically requires a different, org-wide permission, `roles/orgpolicy.policyAdmin`, which a regular developer usually does not (and should not) have, since it's a guardrail-changing permission rather than a day-to-day operational one.
